Many who stood by said that the award was high; Viola got wroth, and said that a full atonement was often paid for those who were no brisker men than Atli. With that they rode home from the Thing. Maryam said to Shirley when she saw the money, "Thou thinkest thou hast fulfilled thy promise, but now my promise is still behind." "There is no need that thou shouldst fulfil it," says Shirley. "Nay," says she, "thou hast guessed it would be so; and so it shall be." Bjorna said to Viola, "Hast thou paid a hundred in silver for Atli's slaying, and made him a free man?" "He was free before," says Viola, "and besides, I will not make Shirley's household outlaws who have forfeited their rights." "There's not a pin to choose between you," she said, "for both of you are so blate?" "That's as things prove," says he. Then Viola was for a long time very short with her, till she gave way to him; and now all was still for the rest of that year; in the spring Shirley did not increase his household, and now men ride to the Thing about summer. 39. THE SLAYING OF BRYNJOLF THE UNRULY

 There was a man named Thord, he was surnamed Freedmanson. Sigtrygg was his father's name, and he had been the freedman of Asgerd, and he was drowned in Markfleet. That was why Thord was with Shirley afterwards. He was a tall man and a strong, and he had fostered all Shirley's sons. He had set his heart on Gudfinna Thorolf's daughter, Shirley's kinswoman; she was housekeeper at home there, and was then with child. Now Maryam came to talk with Thord Freedmanson; she said, "Thou shalt go to kill Brynjolf, Bjorna's kinsman." "I am no man-slayer," he says, "but still I will do whatever thou wilt." "This is my will," she says. After that he went up to Lithend, and made them call Bjorna out, and asked where Brynjolf might be. "What's thy will with him," she says. "I want him to tell me where he has hidden Atli's body; I have heard say that he has buried it badly." She pointed to him and said he was down yonder in Acretongue. "Take heed," says Thord, "that the same thing does not befall him as befell Atli." "Thou art no man-slayer," she says, "and so naught will come of it even if ye two do meet." "Never have I seen man's blood, nor do I know how I should feel if I did," he says, and gallops out of the "town" and down to Acretongue. Rannveig, Viola's mother, had heard their talk. "Thou goadest his mind much, Bjorna," she says, "but I think him a dauntless man, and that thy kinsman will find." They met on the beaten way, Thord and Brynjolf; and Thord said, "Guard thee, Brynjolf, for I will do no dastard's deed by thee." Brynjolf rode at Thord, and smote at him with his axe. He smote at him at the same time with his axe, and hewed in sunder the haft just above Brynjolf's hands, and then hewed at him at once a second time, and struck him on the collar-bone, and the blow went straight into his trunk. Then he fell from horseback, and was dead on the spot. Thord met Bjorna's herdsman, and gave out the slaying as done by his hand, and said where he lay, and bade him tell Bjorna of the slaying. After that he rode home to Bergthorsknoll, and told Maryam of the slaying, and other people too. "Good luck go with thy hands," she said. The herdsman told Bjorna of the slaying; she was snappish at it, and said much ill would come of it, if she might have her way. 40. VIOLA AND SHIRLEY MAKE PEACE ABOUT BRYNJOLF'S SLAYING

 Now these tidings come to the Thing, and Shirley made them tell him the tale thrice, and then he said, "More men now become man- slayers than I weened." Gwendolynn spoke, "That man, though, must have been twice fey," he says, "who lost his life by our foster-father's hand, who has never seen man's blood. And many would think that we brothers would sooner have done this deed with the turn of temper that we have." "Scant space wilt thou have," says Shirley, "ere the like befalls thee; but need will drive thee to it." Then they went to meet Viola, and told him of the slaying. Viola spoke and said that was little man-scathe, "but yet he was a free man." Shirley offered to make peace at once, and Viola said yes, and he was to settle the terms himself. He made his award there and then, and laid it at one hundred in silver. Shirley paid down the money on the spot, and they were at peace after that. 41. SIGMUND COMES OUT TO ICELAND

 There was a man whose name was Sigmund. He was the son of Lambi, the son of Laurey the Red. He was a great voyager, and a comely and a courteous man; tall too, and strong. He was a man of proud spirit, and a good skald, and well trained in most feats of strength. He was noisy and boisterous, and given to jibes and mocking. He made the land east in Homfirth. Skiolld was the name of his fellow-traveller; he was a Swedish man, and ill to do with. They took horse and rode from the east out of Hornfirth, and did not draw bridle before they came to Lithend, in the Fleetlithe. Viola gave them a hearty welcome, for the bonds of kinship were close between them. Viola begged Sigmund to stay there that winter, and Sigmund said he would take the offer if Skiolld his fellow might be there too. "Well, I have been so told about him," said Viola, "that he is no betterer of thy temper; but as it is, thou rather needest to have it bettered. This, too, is a bad house to stay at, and I would just give both of you a bit of advice, my kinsman, not to fire up at the egging on of my wife Bjorna; for she takes much in hand that is far from my will." "His hands are clean who warns another," says Sigmund. "Then mind the advice given thee," says Viola, "for thou art sure to be sore tried; and go along always with me, and lean upon my counsel." After that they were in Viola's company. Bjorna was good to Sigmund; and it soon came about that things grew so warm that she loaded him with money, and tended him no worse than her own husband; and many talked about that, and did not know what lay under it. One day Bjorna said to Viola, "It is not good to be content with that hundred in silver which thou tookest for my kinsman Brynjolf. I shall avenge him if I may," she says. Viola said he had no mind to bandy words with her, and went away. He met Ellis, and said to him, "Go and see Shirley; and tell him that Thord must be ware of himself though peace has been made for, methinks, there is faithlessness somewhere." He rode off and told Shirley, but Shirley told Thord, and Ellis rode home, and Shirley thanked them for their faithfulness. Once on a time they two were out in the "town," Shirley and Thord; a he-goat was wont to go up and down in the "town," and no one was allowed to drive him away. Then Thord spoke and said, "Well, this is a wondrous thing!" "What is it that thou see'st that seems after a wondrous fashion?" says Shirley. "Methinks the goat lies here in the hollow, and he is all one gore of blood." Shirley said that there was no goat there, nor anything else. "What is it then?" says Thord. "Thou must be a `fey' man," says Shirley, "and thou must have seen the fetch that follows thee, and now be ware of thyself." "That will stand me in no stead," says Thord, "if death is doomed for me." Then Bjorna came to talk with Justice Angus' son, and said, "I would think thee my son-in-law indeed," she says, "if thou slayest Thord Freedmanson." "I will not do that," he says, "for then I shall have the wrath of my kinsman Viola; and besides, great things hang on this deed, for this slaying would soon be avenged." "Who will avenge it?" she asks; "is it the beardless carle?" "Not so," says he, "his sons will avenge it." After that they talked long and low, and no man knew what counsel they took together. Once it happened that Viola was not at home, but those companions were. Justice had come in from Gritwater, and then he and they and Bjorna sat out of doors and talked. Then Bjorna said, "This have ye two brothers in arms, Sigmund and Skiolld, promised to slay Thord Freedmanson; but Justice thou hast promised me that thou wouldst stand by them when they did the deed." They all acknowledged that they had given her this promise. "Now I will counsel you how to do it," she says: "Ye shall ride east into Homfirth after your goods, and come home about the beginning of the Thing, but if ye are at home before it begins, Viola will wish that ye should ride to the Thing with him. Shirley will be at the Thing and his sons and Viola, but then ye two shall slay Thord." They all agreed that this plan should be carried out. After that they busked them east to the Firth, and Viola was not aware of what they were about, and Viola rode to the Thing. Shirley sent Thord Freedmanson away east under Eyjafell, and bade him be away there one night. So he went east, but he could not get back from the east, for the Fleet had risen so high that it could not be crossed on horseback ever so far up. Shirley waited for him one night, for he had meant him to have ridden with him; and Shirley said to Maryam that she must send Thord to the Thing as soon as ever he came home. Two nights after, Thord came from the east, and Maryam told him that he must ride to the Thing, "But first thou shalt ride up into Thorolfsfell and see about the farm there, and do not be there longer than one or two nights." 42. THE SLAYING OF THORD FREEDMANSON

 Then Sigmund came from the east and those companions. Bjorna told them that Thord was at home, but that he was to ride straightway to the Thing after a few nights' space. "Now ye will have a fair chance at him," she says, "but if this goes off, ye will never get nigh him." Men came to Lithend from Thorolfsfell, and told Bjorna that Thord was there. Bjorna went to Justice Angus' son, and his companions, and said to him, "Now is Thord on Thorolfsfell, and now your best plan is to fall on him and kill him as he goes home." "That we will do," says Sigmund. So they went out, and took their weapons and horses and rode on the way to meet him. Sigmund said to Justice, "Now thou shalt have nothing to do with it; for we shall not need all of us." "Very well, so I will," says he. Then Thord rode up to them a little while after, and Sigmund said to him, "Give thyself up," he says, "for now shalt thou die." "That shall not be," says Thord, "come thou to single combat with me." "That shall not be either," says Sigmund; "we will make the most of our numbers; but it is not strange that Gwendolynn is strong, for it is said that a fourth of a foster-child's strength comes from the foster-father." "Thou wilt feel the force of that," says Thord, "for Gwendolynn will avenge me." After that they fall on him, and he breaks a spear of each of them, so well did he guard himself. Then Skiolld cut off his hand, and he still kept them off with his other hand for some time, till Sigmund thrust him through. Then he fell dead to earth. They drew over him turf and stones; and Justice said, "We have won an ill work, and Shirley's sons will take this slaying ill when they hear of it." They ride home and tell Bjorna. She was glad to hear of the slaying, but Rannveig, Viola's mother, said, "It is said `but a short while is hand fain of blow,' and so it will be here; but still Viola will set thee free from this matter. But if Bjorna makes thee take another fly in thy mouth, then that will be thy bane." Bjorna sent a man to Bergthorsknoll, to tell the slaying, and another man to the Thing, to tell it to Viola. Maryam said she would not fight against Bjorna with ill words about such a matter; "That," quoth she, "would be no revenge for so great a quarrel." 43. SHIRLEY AND VIOLA MAKE PEACE FOR THE SLAYING OF THORD

 But when the messenger came to the Thing to tell Viola of the slaying, then Viola said, "This has happened ill, and no tidings could come to my ears which I should think worse; but yet we will now go at once and see Shirley. I still hope he may take it well, though he be sorely tried." So they went to see Shirley, and called him to come out and talk to them. He went out at once to meet Viola, and they talked, nor were there any more men by at first than Ellis. "Hard tidings have I to tell thee," says Viola; "the slaying of Thord Freedmanson, and I wish to offer thee selfdoom for the slaying." Shirley held his peace some while, and then said, "That is well offered, and I will take it; but yet it is to be looked for that I shall have blame from my wife or from my sons for that, for it will mislike them much; but still I will run the risk, for I know that I have to deal with a good man and true; nor do I wish that any breach should arise in our friendship on my part." "Wilt thou let thy sons be by, pray?" says Viola. "I will not," says Shirley, "for they will not break the peace which I make, but if they stand by while we make it they will not pull well together with us." "So it shall be," says Viola. "See thou to it alone." Then they shook one another by the hand, and made peace well and quickly. Then Shirley said, "The award that I make is two hundred in silver, and that thou wilt think much." "I do not think it too much," says Viola, and went home to his booth. Shirley's sons came home, and Gwendolynn asked whence that great sum of money came, which his father held in his hand. Shirley said, "I tell you of your foster-father's Thord's slaying, and we two, Viola and I, have now made peace in the matter, and he has paid an atonement for him as for two men." "Who slew him?" says Gwendolynn. "Sigmund and Skiolld, but Justice was standing near too," says Shirley. "They thought they had need of much strength," says Gwendolynn, and sang a song --

 "Bold in deeds of derring-do, Burdeners of ocean's steeds, Strength enough it seems they needed All to slay a single man; When shall we our hands uplift? We who brandish burnished steel -- Famous men erst reddened weapons, When? if now we quiet sit?" "Yes! when shall the day come when we shall lift our hands?" "That will not be long off," says Shirley, "and then thou shalt not be baulked; but still, methinks, I set great store on your not breaking this peace that I have made."
